utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. All the accused are here. All the Defence teams are here, minus Ms. Condon and Mr. Sarapa. Prosecution is Mr. McCloskey and Mr. Vanderpuye. Yes, before we ask you for preliminaries, when dealing with Witness 45 yesterday you remember that we gave our decision on the Madam Fauveau request. There is also, with regard to this witness, a request for putting in place the protective measures of image distortion and pseudonym. Are there any objections from any one of you to the granting of these protective measures? I hear none. So we grant these protective measures in respect to Witness number 45. All right. In preliminaries? Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, Mr. President. We had an issue with a -- a minor issue with the for six months we have been told by the Bench --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: The present witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: For six months we have been told by the Bench that we should endeavour when at all possible to communicate was Prosecution and the Prosecution should communicate with us in order to work things out. We had a minor, simple issue. We worked that out. We thought we worked that out. We both agreed, not only the Prosecution, but all Defence teams, that we only ask for two minutes to talk to this witness to clarify one issue, not ex parte, but with members of the Defence and members of the Prosecution. That request, that simple request got denied. I don't know if I can ask you questions, but I don't know what rationale. If you want us to work together, we will; if you want us to waste our time, we're not going to do it. And with all due request, that's all I've got to say. You denied our request, a joint request by the Prosecution and the Defence to be able to take a few minutes to alleviate what we believe to be at issue that didn't need to crop up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have to stop you because we haven't had any request and we haven't denied anything. What are you talking about?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I apologise. We asked the court officers to talk to the Judges and maybe ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There must have been a big failure in communication, Mr. Meek. When we were spoken to there were two things that we made clear. First, that's none of our business, we don't want to get involved. This is not something in which we should be even -- we should be involved in the least. And the second thing is that we thought you had enough time to discuss. If you want more time, we'll give you more time to discuss. But that's about it. I mean, we don't want to get involved in the issue at all and we don't want to hear any submissions on the issue.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Okay. Then maybe there has been. Let me explain it very briefly. We simply requested, the Prosecution and the Defence, that we have two minutes to speak with the witness now, before she comes in, and it can alleviate up to two hours of cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No problem with two minutes. We were told you needed 10 minutes or so. But if you want two minutes, we'll go out and we'll come back, but otherwise we don't want to hear submissions on what's going on between you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I think frankly you could stay here, we could just go out. She's in the waiting-room, correct? Peter? It's up to you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, we go out. I think it's ... --- Break taken at 2.29 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me, on behalf of the Trial Chamber make something clear. I said earlier on that there must have been some miscommunication. We have had a chance to confirm, the four of us, with the officer, the legal officer also. We had made it clear that we didn't want to hear or be involved in the process that you were discussing amongst you because we were of the opinion that it shouldn't have even been brought to our attention for -- to an extent. But we also made it clear that although we shouldn't be asked for authorisation, we don't want to be involved in that, you will have all the time necessary if you need to discuss amongst yourselves. So this was what went wrong. Yeah, and perhaps we are to blame for that miscommunication. All right. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Mr. President, Your Honours, I would like to thank you for your indulgence and cooperation, and because she had already taken the oath we felt we needed to ask that permission, otherwise we wouldn't have that issue. Thank you for your cooperation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can understand that too, because we come from different jurisdictions and sometimes these things happen. And that is understandable. So, anything else? Can we bring in Ms. Gilleece.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Gilleece. Please make yourself comfortable and let's proceed with your testimony. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, please. Good afternoon Your Honours, good afternoon, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Ms. Gilleece. First I thought I should let the Court know that with regard to the provision of the documents that Ms. Gilleece had with her yesterday, they have been copied and provided to counsel. Ms. Gilleece, I just want to let you know that has the President indicated we have all at times difficulties with our memories and to the extent that you are not able to recall or remember something, if you need to resort to your notes, you can do that with leave of the Court. You ask, and to the extent it is permitted then you will be allowed to do that. So I just wanted to let you know that, and I guess we can pick up where we left off yesterday. I think I had asked you last whether or not you were able to receive an acknowledgement with the respect to the rights that you had informed Mr. Pandurevic and Mr. Sarapa about in relation to this conversation that occurred on the 2nd of October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did receive acknowledgement that both gentlemen understood the rights each time I had given them to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Following your having given Mr. Pandurevic those rights, did there come a time where he actually provided you with certain information?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And to the best of your recollection, can you tell us what information he provided you with?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He provided me with information of some of thinks activities during 1995 specifically July of 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And can you tell us what he told you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He was concerned with a report done by Rick Butler of the MAT [phoen] team that appeared on the internet. His concerns were that Mr. Butler's conclusions were incomplete and he came to the wrong conclusions because he had misinformation. And took things out of context, were Mr. Pandurevic's feelings.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he direct your attention to particular issues that he found that Mr. Butler had incorrectly concluded upon?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was specifically a handwritten report that Mr. Butler refers to, and it's about the killing of pigs, and Mr. Pandurevic stated that the -- the report actually -- the actual report would -- let me just rephrase this. The report actually referred to the 28th Division of the Muslims killing pigs in the area. Nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he refer your attention to a specific term or term of art?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic had brought two books with him, pretty thick books. If I could just refer to my notes, I can get the names of the books.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With the Court's leave, may she refer to her notes?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The first book was -- pardon my mispronunciation. Vojni Leksikon, copyright 1981, published in Belgrade, Serbia. That was a military lexicon and the other one was military encyclopedia, volume 10, copyright 1975, published in Belgrade, Serbia, by Universal Books. There was a term called -- I'm sure my pronunciation is wrong. A-s-a-n-a-c-n-a [sic]. Mr. Pandurevic advised that the term of cleansing the terrain is "asanacija," and it was defined on page 36 of Vojna Enciklopedija. The term is also handwritten on a document that Rick Butler had referred to in his report.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, the document that you are referring to, was that identified by Mr. Pandurevic as a handwritten report?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he said it was a handwritten report and it was dated the 15th of July, 1992, at 200 -- 2 -- 2000 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did he say anything more about that term, or is that the extent of the conversation that you had with respect to it?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: During the -- our discussions, I'm not -- I was not familiar then, nor am I now, with the particulars of this case, so Mr. Pandurevic would jump around a bit and I would just take the information and write it down. That's why the investigative note is not in any kind of concise or doesn't really flow. It jumps around a bit. So if I was to look at my notes here, he also spoke about the -- his -- the zone was also one of the terms that he brought up from the book also, that that was also one of the issues of concern that he had.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. When you say zone, are you referring to -- well, did he refer you to a particular definition of the term "zone" within the context of his zone of responsibility or something of that nature?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, he did, if you will just bear with me one second.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She is checking, Mr. Vanderpuye, reading through the transcript one gets the impression which could be the wrong impression, I don't know. This is why I'm raising this, that these two books that Mr. Pandurevic allegedly brought with him and to which he referred ...

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, I'm sorry. I'm ready when you are, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it does become much clearer then when you read again and again what -- okay. I think it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. I may have missed the -- the issue. I just wanted it -- is it that it's not clear in the record which ...

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That was perhaps not 100 clear. But I think more or less it is the distinction between the Butler papers or whatever documents, and the books, there was some confusion in my mind. But I think, having read it again, it can stay as it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mr. Pandurevic explained that on page 716 of Vojni Leksikon, it says that the sone of intelligence has no other zone of attack. Pandurevic had no zone of responsibility, according to the definitions. And the schools where the POWs were accommodated were not under his control. He also then stated that the term "zone" is defined again on page 709 of the same book. He did allow our interpreter to read the book at the table and she confirmed what was on both pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And she confirmed that had to you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Pandurevic mention anything with respect to his presence or absence from Srebrenica at around the time of its fall?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said he was not Srebrenica at the time of the fall, that he actually had a zone of responsibility and he was 40 -- 40 kilometres away, I believe. Let me just check that. His duties specific to Srebrenica were 40 kilometres from his brigade. That's what he said it was, and then later he mentioned a few things that he had been in -- he gave us a few dates and times specific to where he was and what his actions were.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And do you recall those dates? And if you need to refresh your recollection, just let us know if that's what you -- you've done or you need to do?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I'll just refresh in a moment, here. He was emphatic that on the 14th and 15th of July 1995 he was not present in Srebrenica. He -- on the -- on the 12th of July 1995 the Drina Corps marched towards Zepa. He did say that he attended a meeting on the 11th of July, 1995, in Bratunac with Krstic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did he tell you what the subject matter of that meeting was or among the things that were discussed at that particular meeting?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, at the meeting he said that -- he had spoke to Mladic and he had asked Mladic not to move the units and he suggested that they contact the Muslim 28th Division. But he felt that his proposal was refused as unnecessary -- an unnecessary philosophy and then that was not taken on. They also went over something about concerning the command at that meeting with Krstic and Mladic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Pandurevic indicate to you anything with regard to the movements of his units with respect to Zepa in particular?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you -- the witness answers this question. The last part of her previous answer or her last answer, they also went over something about concerning the command at that meeting with Krstic and Mladic. Can you be more specific because this is, I feel, very generic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That's all I have in my notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And is that all you can recall at this time?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do know there was a change of command and Zivanovic was no longer in command, Krstic was, is what -- that was the change of command that they were referring to. Krstic took over and Zivanovic was going on a rest.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did -- I think I had asked a question ...

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerned with Mr. Pandurevic's movements of his -- his people, he said that his movements were not relevant and they made classical movements toward Zepa.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And --

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 15th he said that he went to the forward command post at a place called Krevaca [phoen], which I recorded phonetically, and that's where he met Krstic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: With respect to these movements towards Zepa, I think you used the term classical movements?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Were you able to ascertain what was meant by that?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I took it to mean classical military movements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Pandurevic indicate when it was, if at all, that he left Zepa?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said on the 15th of July he had met with Krstic and he got approval at about 12.00 p.m. to head towards Srebrenica on the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, did he indicate, if anything, had occurred between the time that he left Zepa on his way back -- did you say Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yeah, he pulled out from Zepa and he was headed towards Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Do you know if he had plans to go to Zvornik?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have to refer to my notes here.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. If you could refer to your notes. Let me just refer you to page 4. Fourth paragraph down.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, on -- I physically don't know where he said, but I put on his return from Zepa to Zvornik. Obviously to go to Srebrenica, he went through Zvornik. And both his brigade and battalion were jeopardised and they had to fight with 7.000 armed soldiers. He was in the main conflict and on the morning of the 15th of July received information that the Muslims wanted to negotiate. The contact person was Semso Muminovic. That's also when he said there was a big rumour that Naser Oric was going to be -- come with the 28th Muslim Brigade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: All right. So did you have some discussion with Mr. Pandurevic about Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We did, because I was pretty familiar with Mr. Oric and his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Ask can you till us?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The witness is kindly asked to move away from the microphone for the benefit of the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The witness will kindly comply.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us in substance what the discussion was with respect to Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said Mr. Pandurevic advised that when this rumour came about that Naser was coming towards them. It was very -- it was almost impossible to keep people focused, because there was such legend, lore, and myth surrounding Mr. Oric and has capabilities. It was simply unbelievable, and it was very hard to keep it inside and then focussed on the task at hand of holding the area they were supposed to hold.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, you had indicated that there was a person that -- that Mr. Pandurevic indicated that he was in contact with, Semso Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Can you tell us a little bit about the conversation concerning him?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pandurevic had said that he had spoken to Mr. Muminovic and that he had let some -- let me just check this. He agreed -- at one point they agreed to allow a status quo situation. That was on the 15th of July, 1995. Then in the morning Muminovic called from a loud-speaker and Pandurevic allowed a lot of people to pass on the 16th of July, 1995. Pandurevic submitted a report on the 16th of July stating that he had allowed a column to pass through. On the 17th Pandurevic made contact again with Muminovic of the 28th Muslim Division. Pandurevic allowed another group of Muslims to pass through. This time he said it was a group of Muslim teenagers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Let me ask you to slow down a little bit so that the interpreters can keep up with you, and we can follow what you are saying, if you could. If you could continue, I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's okay. He also said that when he spoke -- he spoke about Mr. Muminovic and he had already -- Mr. Muminovic had testified at The Hague trial and would be testifying again at Obrenovic at his upcoming trial.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Was that the extent of the conversation you had with Mr. Pandurevic about Mr. Muminovic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe he spoke to him recently. Let me just -- I mean, recent to the time I was speaking to him, so let me just check that. Oh, he had spoken to him a month prior to our meeting is when he had last spoken to Muminovic via telephone. So he was in contact with Muminovic. That would be in October of 2001. Or the month prior, actually, September.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did Mr. Pandurevic indicate to you whether or not he had information about prisoners of war, POWs, in the zone of -- or zone of combat in which he was engaged?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mentioned on the 22nd of July that he had 23 soldiers taken prisoner, POWs. He had asked the commission for exchange to assist as soon as possible and he asked for instruction from them. He received nothing in writing, only by phone. Pandurevic was told to send the POWs to Bakovici [phoen] for an exchange. There was no order issued concerning that. And he also did mention that there were plenty of rumours circulating that there were executions going on but at that time he said there were rumours going on about everything, that nothing really could be trusted. There were all kinds of rumours circulating throughout everything.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he indicate to you whether or not he had received any official reports regarding executions?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just check a second. The only thing that I can recall that he mentioned was that he had said that some of his units were being linked to Obrenovic's activities and Obrenovic was charged with killing POWs on the 14th and 15th; however, he was not at that time sure if that was true or not. He did not have any knowledge of POWs being killed, other than rumour control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he tell you whether or not he had received reports about Muslim prisoners in that area?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very similar, the prisoners were being -- he had -- I wouldn't call it a report. He again -- let me just review my notes a second because it does jump around a bit. At one point he mentioned about POWs accommodated at -- at schools. But they were not under his control. He doesn't go any further, he -- he's not as strong as to say there is official reports. He does speak about rumours, that there is rumours that POWs are detained in schools and had been killed. He was just adamant that if, in fact, there were prisoners there, they were not under his control.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did he, in the course of your conversation, refer to a recording that was taken about the 15th of July, 1995? I just want --

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And let me just ask, without naming the participants of the conversation, could you tell us what the subject matter of that conversation was?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He spoke about a recording. He didn't say how he came to know about that. But on the recording they speak about three and a half thousand packages, meaning people. Request for aid to help with the people is made. A call was made to one general but he was not available. He was directed to call another general, but no one had called Mr. Pandurevic, so Pandurevic -- which was adamant that he had no official information concerning those packages or people. He did say you know who would be able to bring three and a half thousand people and accommodate then.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did he specifically -- well -- define packages as used in that conversation as people?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, does this represent the totality of the conversation that you had with Mr. Pandurevic and Mr. Sarapa and General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And were there other things that you spoke about that you did not take note of?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Since there was -- the main intent of the meeting with Zivanovic was to -- for team 6 -- not for team 6 but for team 9 to forward what our goal was to get more evidence concerning our case. So we spoke at length, Mr. Pandurevic and I, about the food, things that you did to make a connection so that people will trust you and then hopefully be able to trust you with items that we needed for evidence on our case. So we discussed the food, we discussed, I believe, he had small children. His brother was the person who had driven them to the appointment. We discussed the weather. Many times I was taught the word "polako" which is slow down. Mr. Zivanovic is an avid bee raiser or he has bee huts. We discussed that a lot. There were a lot of things that we discussed, and we did discuss some issues regarding Kamenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, during the time that you had this conversation with Mr. Pandurevic did you -- did you say anything to him or do anything to give him the impression that he would receive some sort of benefit if he spoke to you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. The only -- yeah, the benefit I told him is, I would try to record as -- as accurately as possible, and I would pass an accurate message to Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And is that what he requested of you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And aside from that, did you do anything or make any promises to him with respect to the disposition of any matter that might be pending before the Tribunal or that might be brought?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Did anybody else that you were with take any such action?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, did anybody else besides you ask any clarification-types of questions of Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Cooper would have, the military analyst that was with me.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, aside from clarification types of questions did either you or Mr. Cooper or anybody else ask Mr. Pandurevic questions in order to uncover information that he hadn't otherwise shared with you? Investigatory types of questions.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, other than clarification on how to spell something, maybe the interpreter to repeat something and how it was said. Mr. Cooper would ask things to clarify terminology. We did not ask the normal investigatory questions other than clarification of his statements.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Now, at the time you spoke to Mr. Pandurevic, were you taking notes contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think you indicated Mr. Cooper also took notes contemporaneously?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, usually the interpreter myself and whoever is present takes notes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And did these notes work their way into this note that you have referring to, this investigative note?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, at the end of the meeting I collect all the notes when we get together by ourselves. We go over to make sure nothing has been missed. I then draft a -- a report, or in this case an investigative note, and then it's typed up and the notes are shredded. And the only existence of a note is this investigative, and then the memo that I was told to send to Patrick Lopez-Terres.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. Now, with respect to the note that you prepared, is it fair to say that it incorporates the substance of the notes that you took contemporaneously or, I should say, that were taken contemporaneously by you and Mr. Cooper?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell us just that, I guess, the record is more complete when it was about that you prepared this investigative note that you are referring to?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would have prepared on the 6th or 7th. The actual body of it, I ran into an issue of -- because -- this was the first time something like this had happened. When I returned I'd obviously spoken to someone who was on a sealed indictment. I found that out on my return. Then there was some discussion as to how it was going to be recorded, the body would be as it stands, but was it going to be a report, investigative note, and it was determined that it would -- a memo, it was determined to be an investigative note.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And you believe you prepared that on the 6th or so of October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: In any event, several days after the actual conversation?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, definitely.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Just bear with me for one moment, if -- if the Court would just bear with me for a sec. All right. Thank you very much, Ms. Gilleece. I don't have any further questions at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm not about to cross-examine. I'm about to inform you of what is likely to be a change in the programme. I was going to cross-examine this witness first, but in the light of the evidence I have heard, I want to talk to my client about the strategy of cross-examination to follow, and Ms. Fauveau has kindly agreed that she will cross-examine this witness first. Depending on how long she is, if it takes us to a break, I want to speak to my client before I proceed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We will give you all the time you require.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau. Anyone else would be cross-examining this witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: We may, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So Madam Fauveau, will you go first? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Madam, you worked in the OTP office, your primary duties were to investigate on crimes committed against Serbs; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And as part of your duties you received many documents from the organs of the Republic of Srpska, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I have.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you also received the journal written by Naser Oric; is that right?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... one that was attributed to him, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And that agenda or journal you received it in the month of February, 2002?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware off the top of my head if that's when I received it, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D174, please. I am terribly sorry this document is not translated, but I am absolutely certain that we can certainly work from the document in Serbo Croatian. What I am interested in is the date, you can certainly see the date of the 20th of February, 2002, on this document?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And you can also see that your name is written at the bottom. It says, "Ms. Gilleece, investigator for the ICTY Banja Luka field office"?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, my signature appears up in the top right corner, ma'am, dated 20 February 2002. That's definitely me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the second page of this document, please. I am going to read the portion that is after -- that is written after number 1 so that we can translate it or that it can be translated for the benefit of all the parties in this courtroom. Diary of Naser Oric with two photographs.

utterances.speaker: THE FRENCH INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Oric with two pictures.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Madam, do you recognise receiving this journal from Naser Oric that day?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just to be clear, I received that from the Republic of Srpska officials. They attribute that had that diary was Mr. Oric's. I did not meet with Mr. Oric to receive that. The Republic of Srpska, their position was that it was his diary. I had not yet authenticated that or determined what exactly was turned over to me.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And, in fact, when you came back you put this diary somewhere without analysing it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, that would be -- I did not analyse it, but I turned it over to our intelligence analyst, Michael Sporluk, because he could read B/C/S - I could not and do not - and he provided an assessment.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown 5D173, please. And this document also could be shown in English, please. This document is only available in the English version. Witness, I will let you examine this document. Is it correct to say that this document is referring to the diary that Republic of Srpska thought belonged to Naser Oric or was his?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think it is the one that I had retrieved, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And if we read the last paragraph of this document, which is a document stemming from the OTP, this diary is -- was found in your office on the 8th of July, 2004, or, rather, more than one year after you left the OTP. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know I turned that over to Michael Sporluk and Gamini Wijeyesinghe, and I was doing a lot of travelling. I would come back with the packages and I'd turn them over to Gamini and Mr. Sporluk to send for processing and iffing [phoen]. I was not aware that that was left in any cabinet in the team 9 area. I know when that document came in it was read by Michael Sporluk to exhaustion. And that was when I first came back. So I'm quite surprised to -- to see this note.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, are you telling us that you did not know that this note existed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm going to object to my learned friend's question. I don't think there is a basis for it and I don't see what the particular relevance of the line of questioning is. She hasn't identified a source of the information with which she has confronted the witness, and if -- you can read from the document itself, it contains a relatively accusatory language, but there doesn't seem to be any source to which it's attributable, and the witness has already indicated she is surprised to see it, so I think the question is kind of superfluous in the line of questions. Line of questioning is irrelevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just a moment, I will consult with my colleagues

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In asking your question initially you mentioned that this diary or you suggested by reference to this document to the witness that it was found in her office on the 8th of July. The document does not say that. The document says that the diary plus, et cetera, were discovered in a cabinet in team 9 area. Was Mr. Sporluk part of team 9?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, as was Mr. -- actually, he was part of the intelligence analyst team, and Mr. Wijeyesinghe was a part of team 9.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. So perhaps now you can put your question again, Ms. Fauveau. Or rephrase your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Witness, did you know that there was a problem with this diary? Did somebody contact you from the OTP after you left regarding the diary of Naser Oric?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not specifically the diary. They contacted me about materials from the Republic of Srpska which I had turned over to Mr. Wijeyesinghe and I told them I had turned them over to him.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it true that there were certain documents which had been received from the Republic of Srpska and which had not been properly treated at the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: According to this note you put before me, it appears that could be the case, ma'am.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye. We had anticipated this question, basically. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I would object to the question. I know that it's been answered already. But the line of question with respect to the proper handling of this material, I don't think even a foundation has been laid in order to justify the question. And once again, I don't know what the relevance of that is to the witness's testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, we have given due consideration to your objection. We do see some relevance to the point raised by the -- or the point that Ms. Fauveau seeks to pursue. So please answer the question. I will repeat the question for her. She answered part. Is it true that there were certain documents which had been received from RS and which had not been properly treated at the Office of the Prosecutor. And your answer started, "According to this note you put before me, it appears that could be the case, ma'am." But did you finish your answer or did you wish to add more to it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I do know that when being questioned, Mesi Manas [phoen] on the trial of Naser Oric was asked about some iffing and discovery issuing, and she mentioned my name, that I didn't process documents appropriately. However, on further questions she said that there was an investigation being conducted at the Tribunal and there had been no conclusion to that. I was not contacted other than by Ken Klora [phoen] to ask about documents, and I told them what I had done with them, and that was the end of it as far as I was concerned. And then I was told. I was quite surprised that Resin [phoen] answered that way in front of the Tribunal and that is on record and on the internet and that could be what the good counsel is referring to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Shall we move to another subject, Ms. Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Mr. President. As far as I'm concerned I have finished. I have no other question to ask.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. Just a few questions, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. In fact, the name of the investigator or the person that testified in connection with your discovery process concluded that it was negligent what you did; isn't that correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: She certainly concluded that, sir, but no one else.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No one else that you know of?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No one else that I am aware of at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now let me go back quickly to the October 2nd 2001 meeting with Mr. Pandurevic. You stated that you had read him his rights basically four to six times during the six or eight-hour meeting that you had, correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That would be correct, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why do you that?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because he was discussing issues of concern from 1995, and I wanted to make sure he knew that anything he was telling me I would have to repeat here to the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, could you have easily, during that eight or so hour meeting with him, called team 6 to inform them you were meeting with Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, I couldn't have. I had a mobile phone that did not work in the Republic of Srpska in that area. Because we did consider that. We would not have trusted the phones - I don't even know if there was a phone - in the restaurant. And the radio in the UN vehicle actually didn't work either, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. And can you tell me where your notes are from that meeting, your actual notes that you took?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I stated earlier, I shredded them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, did you also tell us from what I recall that you were unfamiliar with the events of Srebrenica and you were just talking to General Zivanovic about what occurred in 1992 and 1993, the atrocities that may have occurred against Serbs, correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right. I had a vague idea of had a happened in 1995 just from the -- CNN during 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Ms. Gilleece, I disagree with you on that point. You have more than a vague understanding of what happened in Srebrenica, don't you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Today I do, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: No, ma'am. Actually in October of 2001 you did.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You have to understand I'm working on Naser Oric. It's -- everything's 1992, even in my investigative note, I default to 1992. You're so focussed. It's a country that, you know, the culture, the language, I'm very focussed on the events that I need to do for my case. So it was rather foreign to me, the 1995 issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Help me understand this: Did you at all testify in the Krstic case?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Speakers please make pauses.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, in fact I was going to draw your attention. I think you're going too fast and you are not allowing a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I will repeat the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, and Ms. Gilleece, please allow a short pause between question and answer so we don't make the interpreters' lives more difficult than it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did you testify in the General Krstic case in this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: What was that case about?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That case was about General Krstic in 1995, his actions.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In Srebrenica, correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now let me guess, did you he have testify in this case before or after your interview with Mr. Pandurevic in October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So you had some facts or some knowledge or information other than CNN because you had, in fact, testified in the Krstic case four months before you actually met with Mr. Pandurevic, correct?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I had some basic facts as I stated, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you this also: Did you ever discuss with General Zivanovic prior to October 2nd, 2001, anything about Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Before or after your meeting with Mr. Pandurevic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How many times did you meet with General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I met him the first time was April the 12th, 2001. I saw him again on April the 23rd. I would have spoken to him on the phone between those two dates at least once. And then I had spoken to him at least once before to arrange the meeting in October. So I would say two to three times on the phone and twice in person, and that would be the third time in October 2001 as best I can recall, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Other than watching CNN from what you told us and learning something about Srebrenica on CNN, in fact isn't it true that Mr. Zivanovic in those meetings in April of 2001 gave you specific information in connection with Srebrenica in 1995?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: His specific information mainly rallied around the fact that he was not -- he was not involved as a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Did he show you any notes?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He showed me a document that he was relieved of command and Krstic was put into command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Show me the process or tell me about the process in your office when you interview someone who might be considered a suspect?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: You -- when they're considered a suspect you read them your rights, you advise them that they are a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about retention of documents?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not sure I'm understanding your question, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'll clarify it. Thank you for telling me that. If you interview someone who is a potential suspect, did you keep notes on that, do you tape record the conversation or do you just do it by memory and generally try to recollect?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, a suspect you have to videotape. There's pretty strict rules governing a suspect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is that?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For their rights and to protect them.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And do you think that's only here at the ICTY or worldwide?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is at the ICTY.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Don't answer the question. Come on, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Let me ask you this, Ms. Gilleece, if I may. Do you have your notes from your meetings of April 13th and April 23rd or 25th of 2001 with Mr. Zivanovic or General Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I do not.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Do you have your notes, ma'am of the meeting that you had with Mr. Pandurevic, among others, on October 2nd, 2001?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The note -- the investigative note to file that has been articulated in this case is the note I have, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the speakers please slow down.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm asking of your handwritten notes?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, as I stated, the process, I shred them as soon as I memoralise them in this report.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Looking at that memo, can you tell me what date appears on that memo that you wrote this -- this investigative note to file?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is no date that appears which is the day wrote it, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why is there no date on this memo that you wrote?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't put one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yeah, but why not?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the first and only investigative note to file I did at Tribunal. There didn't seem to be a format. This is what I submitted to my superiors and they said that that was the format that was acceptable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: In fact, isn't it true that on October 31st, 2001 you submitted a different summary of your meeting with Mr. Pandurevic on the 2nd of October 2001?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: It wasn't different, it wasn't illuminated. The one to Patrick Lopez-Terres was an internal memo, and that was just to cover that I'd in fact met with Mr. Pandurevic. There was some consternation because I met with Mr. Pandurevic and the SFOR had been hitting houses in Bosnia at the same time. So it seemed a bit odd that the ICTY was paying for his lunch and then looking for him in Bosnia. So Mr. Lopez-Terres asked for a report and that's what I submitted.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Why wouldn't you in this October 31st, 2001 internal memo merely attach your investigative note to file if you had written it prior to the 31st of October?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The purpose of this memo was not to attach the document that was going to be discoverable. This was an internal memo that goes in -- that secretaries file. I would never put evidence -- that's why it speaks of the investigative note so that it can be found, but I wouldn't put it to an internal memo that anybody in the Tribunal may or may not have access to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: That's all I have for this witness at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Apart from Mr. Haynes, anyone else wishes to cross-examine the witness? If not, I suggest we have the break now rather than in 15 minutes' time. We will give you 25 minutes' break. If you need more, Mr. Haynes, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I doubt it, but that's very kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, you should be provided with all the facility to meet in private with your client. We will continue after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Haynes. Have you had time to consult with your client?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, I have a few questions of this witness, but I won't be very long.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It is Ms. Gilleece, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's always wise to check. We speak the same language, so can you wait for the translation of my questions for other people before you respond to it?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yesterday we looked at two documents that I hope you still have with you. Do you?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Did you yourself create both of those documents? That's the memo and the note to investigative file?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And by that do you mean you typed them out yourself or you had somebody type them for you and you checked them?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I typed them out myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And did you check them both for accuracy at the time and again when you prepared for your testimony this week?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did check them for accuracy at the time and then when I prepared for my testimony this week I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were you content at the time you created them that they had no errors in them, either in terms of the transcription of your notes or typographical?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the time I created them I thought they were accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that we're clear, are they the -- the only written records surviving about this conversation on the 2nd of October?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir, they are, to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Now I'm not going to be repetitive, but this was an extraordinarily long meeting, wasn't it, with Mr. Pandurevic, Mr. Zivanovic, Mr. Sarapa, and two of your colleagues?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It probably doesn't matter, but do you recall that, in fact, you left this restaurant at about 10.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew it was --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: She said it yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yesterday she said 7.30. I'm putting a different time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think she lasted until about 10.00 or something like that. Anyway, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Can we clarify, do you recall that you left this restaurant about 10.00 in the evening?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yesterday I said about 7.30, but it wouldn't surprise me if it was about 9.00 or 10.00, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And you said it was a meeting that encompassed, among other things, a pretty long lunch?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, there was food and drink all afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And the conversation that you had involved not just Mr. Pandurevic, but contributions from all of you, a number of people?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And substantially all conducted through translators?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, the principal purpose of your going to the restaurant in Peti Puk was to discuss with Mr. Pandurevic information he could give you that would help you with your investigation. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And he did give you quite a lot of information about the events of 1992 and 1993, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He gave us a -- information of people to contact and about the recovery of the bodies in Kamenica in 1993 because he was on site.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean would you agree that on that, leaving aside Srebrenica of 1995, you probably talked for a good two hours?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir. At least that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very fair of you. And did you make notes of what he told you about Kamenica in 1992 and 1993?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But most of what he had told us we already knew. The new information were names of people to contact to get documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Were those notes ever typed up?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Any reason for that?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: He mainly told us what we had seen on the video of the bodies being recovered in Kamenica. And he gave us names of people. Those were recorded and passed on to other members of the team.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, in terms of the notes you did take, how were they taken? Were they taken in a notebook or on loose sheets of paper?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: A legal pad that's attached at the top and you can flip the pages.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And were they rough notes or long, verbatim conversation?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I usually try to take as much verbatim as I can, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, when you returned you wrote a memo, didn't you, the shorter document you've referred to yesterday?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I -- the investigative note to file, the body of it was typed shortly after I returned within that week. I wasn't advised to write the memo until a later time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it's your evidence therefore then, is it, that the memo of the 31st of October is the second document in time that you created?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And these two documents are the only document you have ever created?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Concerning this incident, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The memo, I have been told by the Prosecution, is a confidential document, and I must treat it as such. But I'd like you, please, if you would have a look at it.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In particular I'd like you to look at the very last sentence.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I thought you might.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's a confidential document. I will read the sentence into the record. It says, "I will forward a detailed investigator's report to team 6 detailing Pandurevic's comments and his explanation."

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, doesn't that make it clear that the longer document was created after the 31st of October?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The body of the longer document was created immediately. The top portion, investigative note to file, wasn't created until after I sent this. You are correct. But I -- the only thing I had to put on was the investigative note to file. As you see on the 31st or as you have read, it's called a -- investigator's report in the memo. After some discussion by my superiors I was told to title it, "Investigative note." I guess I wasn't clear earlier. The body of the longer document was done first. Then I typed the internal memorandum, after some discussion on what -- how to actually call it, it was -- I was told it to make it investigative note, date, event, place, time present. I hope that clarifies it for you, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, thank you for that explanation. Can we now move across to the investigative note to file.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And I want you to look at the very first paragraph of that document, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is creating difficulties for the Trial Chamber, because we don't have this document.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It is really not necessary for you to. I'm going to ask a very simple question.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: In the first paragraph the investigative note to file, what date did you say this meeting took place on?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: October 2nd, 2001.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No. Third line down.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Oh, I'm sorry, I thought you meant in the beginning. In the first paragraph I have it as 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, you told us there were no typos in this. Can you explain why you placed this meeting that you wrote up in October 2001 a year into the future?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I actually did not testify that there were no typos. There are numerous typos. I said at the time I submitted it, I believed there were no typos, sir. Clearly I made a mistake here as I have on other pages of the document with years. In particular I usually have put down 1992 when I meant 1995. And I would correct those if you would allow me.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I'm going to move on now because ---

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think it's the case. I suppose, Mr. Vanderpuye, when you stood up, you wanted to refer to her previous answer which did not acknowledge --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Given the circumstances in -- in which this meeting took place, and the way in which the notes were created and the note to file subsequently created, can I ask you this: Do you accept that whilst you have successfully recorded the substance of this conversation, that the detail of what was said may be subject to correction?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: The detail of the dates would be subject to correction, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. That's very fair. I'm only going to direct you really to those areas about which you have given evidence today. And the first of those is the reference by Mr. Pandurevic to the two legal text-books that he brought with him. I think you will probably find that that's at page 4 of your notes.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: It's right, isn't it, that Mr. Pandurevic's biggest beef, as it were, was with the conclusions of Richard Butler?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And just so that we could place these events in context, this interview took place shortly after the conclusion of the trial of Radoslav Krstic, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And in order to illustrate some of his points, he brought military manuals with him?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was my understanding.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yeah. And he showed you them?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Now, what you've told us that he said was that by reference to those manuals the zone of intelligence has no other zone of attack.

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, did you comprehend that when he said it in October of 2001?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just that the intelligence deals with intelligence and not a zone of attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I mean, does it make any sense to you now?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not really. In the sense that no other zone of attack is, like, not a combat, it is not a tangible item. Intelligence is not tangible. Zone of attack would be tangible is how I took it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you. I don't want to put words into your mouth, but wasn't this what was being said, that the responsibility of the intelligence organ of the army could not be limited by a geographically defined area?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the next section where he said, "Pandurevic had no zone of responsibility according to the definitions." I want to explore what you considered that to mean. Wasn't he saying there that the rules of the army did not recognise the concept of a zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry, can you repeat the question, sir?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes. By reference to the military text-books, he was pointing out to you that army rules did not recognise the concept of a zone of responsibility?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: For intelligence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: No, this is the second item you have mentioned --

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: -- where it says Pandurevic --

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Him self that he no zone that he was adamant that he had no zone of responsibility according to those definitions that were cited. He was very clear about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much, indeed. And I just have one more thing to ask you about. And that's about the slaughter of pigs and asanacija or cleaning the terrain. Do you recall that -- that part of the conversation?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Do you recall now, refreshing your memory from your notes, if you must, that those two ideas were linked in his explanation?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: And that he gave the example of the slaughter of pigs and the responsibility of the army to clear up rotting carcasses as part of their duty of asanacija?

utterances.speaker: EILEEN GILLEECE [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That's very, very helpful of you. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Haynes. I take it there are no further questions, cross-examinations from the Defence. Mr. Vanderpuye, would you like to re-examine the witness?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Gilleece, basically that means that your testimony finishes here. I wish to thank you for having come over to give testimony. And I thank you on behalf of the Tribunal and also on behalf of everyone wish you a safe journey back home.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's start with the Prosecution. Are there any documents you would like to tender?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There are, Mr. President. In particular, we would like to tender what's been marked as P02048.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is it still per -- according to the list that you have circulated?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, it -- it -- yes, it is. I think it's the first item on the list. Now, we had indicated previously at the beginning of the last session that we had reached an understanding with Defence counsel with respect to certain issues that bear upon the evidence in the case, and we would like to tender that document subject to certain redactions that we feel are appropriate to both the probity and the relevance of the material, with the Court's permission.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So any objections on the part of any of the Defence teams to the admission of P02408?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What's the basis of your objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: The basis of the objection is firstly it has not been introduced into evidence. It is simply an aide-memoire. The witness used it to -- to give live evidence. It is her evidence that stands. I quite purposefully pruned my cross-examination to deal only with those matters which she gave in evidence in chief and therefore there is a prejudice by introducing this document now. There are other objections that -- that I will leave others to make, but in my submission, that document has not become admissibility, it hasn't been introduced into evidence, and this is in a way a form of putting in some statement that -- that the witness hasn't come up to proof on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you like to respond to that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: If I may. I think that -- I think Mr. Haynes indeed was very careful with respect to his examination of Ms. Gilleece; however, I do feel that he specifically drew her attention to errors that were made in that report as distinguished from errors that were made that were subject of her testimony, which is a separate issue. In particular, he referred her to the first paragraph, I think, of that report in which he indicated that the meeting was scheduled to occur on the 2nd of October of 2002, which was not the subject of her testimony but was in the content of the report itself, and therefore my view of it is that he has now brought into issue the accuracy and reliability of the notes that were taken themselves as distinguished from the testimony that she related. There are two particular grounds, I think, that support it. One was obviously the attention to whether or not there were typographical errors in the report itself and the second related to the subject matter of the information that she took down whether it was shorthand, long hand, abbreviated, and he specifically asked her whether or not it might be subject to correction or something to that effect. And to that extent I think that he has now made the report a relevant issue as distinguished from her testimony about the information that was related to her by the accused, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: And Mr. McCloskey has also pointed out that it would be obviously, I think, useful to the Court in order to put the testimony that was elicited in context, particularly as I recall -- I don't know if there was a specific request by the Court to see the document, but I know that there was some concern that there was testimony proceeding about the document to which the Court didn't have access. I think my learned friend indicated that it wasn't necessary for the Court at that time to see the document, but I rather disagree and I think it would be helpful to put in context subject matter of the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any further objections from any of the other Defence teams? Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I had thought and understood that these types of statements were not going to come in as a general matter with witnesses, and they can testify, although we have agreed on certain redactions in that statement. But if the Prosecutor wanted to lead other evidence, I would suggest that they should have led that evidence and, as opposed to calling a witness, state your name, and converting her into a 92 ter or whatever witness she may be. She was a live witness. They could have covered it verbatim. She was reading it quite candidly throughout yesterday and most of today as she was flipping the pages. So the statement is unnecessary. I think it's duplicative, and I think it will create a practice that with every witness we can come in and say, Oh, yes, why don't we give his testimony in the Krstic case or in other cases or other statements. Then the Court would just have too much information and it is the testimony of the witness before us that the Court will be required to assess her credibility. But we have an agreement. We would object to it generally but if it does go in, we insist that we stand by our agreement that it be given to the Court in its redacted form.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I just think an important distinction to draw with respect to Mr. Ostojic's argument is that, you know, there may be some validity to his contentions with respect to a statement that is not the statement of an accused. This is a statement that was made by a person who is charged with the events, the subject matter of the statement. It is in effect an admission. It is ostensibly more reliable for that reason. It would otherwise be clearly admissable certainly against that particular accused. There may be some argument with respect to its applicability to other accused that may be implicated or otherwise, but it is certainly, I don't think, an issue, the admissibility of the statement with regard to the declarant in this case. The statement has been available to the Defence, I think, for quite some time now. It wasn't raised in -- in any particular --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I object to that.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone please, for Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You need to repeat all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I will deal with it in a minute. I will let Mr. Vanderpuye finish.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye, you still have the floor.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I believe I was saying that it wasn't raised in any particular way by anyone other than the accused in this case, the subject matter of its admissibility in -- in its -- in a written form as opposed to a testimonial form.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We haven't heard anything from you as yet on the submission that was made, namely that throughout the course of your examination-in-chief you never put this document to her witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: That is correct. And the reason why I didn't do that is because what I sought to elicit from the witness was her present recollection of the statement, aside from the physical document itself, and that I would submit was an intentional act that was followed on our part in order to avoid this very issue. I think Mr. Haynes is mistaken when he says that he's pruned his cross-examination to avoid this issue, because I think, actually, it created the issue by specifically bringing the witness's attention to errors that are contained in that report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think I didn't make myself clear. The submission was if it was your intention throughout to introduce or tender this document at the end, why didn't you make use of it during your examination-in-chief? Or redirect, yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: First, it wasn't my intention all along to tender the document into evidence, which is what I think I -- I -- I am -- I was trying to say. It wasn't at all my intention to tender the document in evidence. It was my intention to elicit the witness's present recollection of the statement that is contained within the document in order to avoid precisely this issue.
