I think the issue has been created, rather, on the contrary, because despite our efforts or my effort to avoid the use of the documents, specific questions were elicited on cross-examination, you could say impugning the witness's credibility with respect to the creation of the duty or the contents that are in it. Specifically in interpretation of its accuracy, dates, details, longhand conversion of the transcribed notes, and the basis and the timing that it was -- the time that it was created. All of those things, I think, now put in issue exactly what it is that we hadn't intended to introduce. That's the reason why I think it's relevant and appropriate to tender it at this point.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, do you wish to wind up?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Not much. I just wish to point out that on the 4th of September we invited the Prosecution to take a witness statement from this witness; if they had done that they could have treated her as a 92 ter witness. This isn't a witness statement, it's a note to file. It could have been used far more extensively to -- to adduce the detail of the conversation. It wasn't. We relied upon that approach, and it simply hasn't gone into evidence and should not now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise you were -- you were standing up again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I do apologise, I know you are about to deliberate on the issue, but I think Mr. Haynes is right, this is not a witness statement. I don't know that even 92 ter would be applicable to this statement in particular because we are talking about a statement about another statement, in effect. And in addition, the statement we are talking about happens to be, in our view, an admission. That is, a statement made by an accused in a case about the circumstances and facts at issue in the case. And so I don't even believe that a 92 ter application would have been appropriate in order to elicit the testimony about the statement that was made by the accused in this case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our conclusion is as follows: We feel that it will not be appropriate to deny outright the Prosecution request to tender this document. We believe that once it is obvious from the proceedings that she was relying on this document, then at least as far as that goes the document should be before the Trial Chamber as well. However, since there is -- there are some arguments which are valid, intrinsically valid, we are giving you the opportunity to consult together, particularly the Ostojic and the Pandurevic -- sorry, not -- the Beara and the Pandurevic Defence teams to consult with the Prosecution, and if you can come to an agreement to the effect of redacting some parts from the document itself, we will admit it with the redacted -- with the redacted parts. Otherwise, we will admit it and then use our discretion, obviously. We are four professional judges here, and we know that our responsibility mainly is directed towards the viva voce evidence that we have heard. All right. And you will come back to us on this at the earliest. Thank you. I'm sure you will find a way. Now, I see you standing again.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I am, unfortunately. There is one other document, and I -- and I would -- I guess I would seek the consent of Defence counsel with respect to this particular one. It is 65 ter 00426. And that is simply the July 15th report -- am I mistaken?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 00329. That's the July 15th report that was made reference to by the accused in the course of his statements to the witness. We -- we would submit that it will be ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question to you. Is there no other witness that you could introduce this document with?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There actually is. But we expect that witness to be called quite far in the future. I would ask if you would entertain admitting it subject to connection at this point. Because I think it's relevant to the subject of this testimony, but that's only -- I would only make that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any objections on the part of the Defence teams? Mr. Haynes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Being realistic, this document is going to go in at some stage but I don't actually recall this witness dealing with this particular exhibit. And it becomes circular. It makes no sense to you at this stage. You might as well wait for somebody who can explain it to you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not really the point, but do you wish to respond to that, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: No, sir.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's deliberate on that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our decision is that we are not admitting it outright. We will just mark it for identification for the time being. And then we'll decide later, in all probability this will be used with some other witness as you stated in any case. So that could supercede and solve the problem. Are you standing up again, Mr. Vanderpuye?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Only to respond "no."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So the Miletic Defence team have got two documents. One is 5D174 and the other one is 5D173. The first one hasn't been translated into English, I take it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right, Mr. President. We will give to the Chamber the translation as soon as it is ready and for the third document the Prosecutor already raised an objection as to the source of this document, but this document was produced by the OTP and it was found on IDS, the general collection, so this is probably a document stemming from the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which document? Because I only have two here. In the transcript it says the third document.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] 5D173.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's not the third, it's the second, for the record. Are there any objections from the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before that, can I ask Madam Fauveau about its -- their relevance or significance to this case?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is the way the Prosecutor conducts its -- his investigation and the way they conduct their investigation, have a certain meaning about the way they lead this investigation and we will object to other documents stemming from the OTP. This why we believe this document is relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you wish -- first of all, are there any objections to the admission of these two documents on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, there is an objection as to the second of the two. I think -- which was identified as 5D173. That's identified as the surrogate sheet, a synopsis/description of evidence. The nature of the objection is that we don't feel it is relevant to the testimony of the witness in this particular case and practices of the OTP are not certainly documented in a synopsis of evidence that was prepared by an unnamed person based upon unknown information, the veracity of which has been untested and otherwise unidentified. So I don't think it should be admitted first on the grounds of relevance and second on the grounds of probity.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: You are not challenging the authenticity, to make sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I will take my learned friend's word for it that it was discovered, I think on EDS, she mentioned. And I have no reason to believe it wasn't generated in a -- by our office or maybe the evidence unit, but I don't think it has any relevance or there is any inherent reliability in the information that is relayed into that document because that document is intended to relay that kind of informing. There would be a report or something of that nature would be far more persuasive and more relevant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I do not know if there is a report written on this incident, but we are not -- it is not in our possession. The Prosecutor has it and he has not sent it to us. In fact, this document should have been sent to us, as to -- all the relevant documents through this witness should have been sent to us and any other person or any other document that is relevant. A journal of Naser Oric is definitely important. So the Prosecutor should have communicated to us a full report. He didn't do so, and this is the only document that I found, so I don't see why this document should not be admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, can I ask you, are you intending call any other evidence in relation to this document, the author of this document? Any other evidence you intend to call with respect to it?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not at this point, but it is quite difficult to answer that question at this point, since I just discovered this document two or three days ago and I did not have time to make an investigation as to this incident.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: And Madam Fauveau, you make the statement that the journal of Naser Oric is definitely important to the case. Earlier you indicated that this evidence was important to demonstrate the approach of the Prosecution office or the failings in the activities of the Prosecutor's office. Can you explain to me your statement that Naser Oric's journal is relevant to the case before us?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it is a question to which I cannot answer. I don't have the diary, I don't know to what period it's referring to. I have no information about that diary. This diary was not sent to us. It was not given to us. I have no information on that diary. However, the fact that this diary exists and that we were not informed of its existence creates a doubt on the documents that the Prosecutor communicated to us up until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Judge Prost, and thank you, Madam Fauveau. Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: I think that I should say in all fairness that I -- I did disclose to Defence counsel that in substance the allegations that are contained within that document was the subject matter of prior testimony and I think in my proofing note I even provided the transcript page, pages, that refer to the specific incident. And I think Mr. Ostojic cross-examined the witness with respect to that. Our position remains, however, that this particular document has no probity to the extent that it is entirely unclear as to what -- on what basis the document was created, who created it and whether or not it is even reliable. Because it is not clear that that document corresponds to the information that was actually the subject of testimony, and I think that if my learned colleague sought to introduce probative, reliable evidence on the Prosecution's practices on the handling of evidence and more appropriately this witness's practices with respect to the handling of evidence, that that could be done through a far more reliable source, which is the sworn testimony of a witness to whom Defence was alerted, not only that the fact that the witness testified, but the subject matter of the witness's testimony and the page numbers upon which it could be found in the relevant transcript. And so that is the basis -- essentially as the basis of the objection to this particular material.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So our position is the following: We wouldn't like to take more time of the sitting to reach a decision. We are not in a position to conclude our deliberations now, so we will postpone the decision until later and let you know. Yes, on 5D173. As regards 5D174, I hear no objections, so that document is marked for identification pending translation, when it will be upgraded to proper. Now, I -- we were informed earlier on that there has been a change in the schedule, and that the next witness will not be Witness number 45, but Mr. Brunborg. And this, I take it, will only be examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't realise we had finished with the exhibits, but following the philosophy of the earlier decision it seems to me in relation to Ms. Gilleece that the internal memorandum should be introduced into evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vanderpuye.

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: There is no be objection to that. I only ask that it be admitted under seal. It is an internal -- is there an objection?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is there a problem with that, Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Well, it's been disclosed to everybody, it's been referred to in evidence. If there was any privilege, I would have thought it would have been waived by now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Why do you require it to be under seal?

utterances.speaker: MR. VANDERPUYE
utterances.text: Well, it is an internal memorandum. It actually came into evidence, really, quite by happenstance because the witness had referred to it yesterday. It certainly wasn't intended to be offered or relied upon in any way. And to the extent that it deals or -- we are concerned about two things. One is the precedent of admitting internal memorandum of the Office of the Prosecutor, and the second, of course, is that it contains information, I think, that should remain in the confines of the Court and not privy to others outside these proceedings. So we don't have a problem with it going into evidence at this point, because clearly it was the subject of it since she -- the witness referred to it, but I think to make it otherwise public would be inappropriate, notwithstanding its reference, the references that have been made to it in the record up until now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Haynes, do you wish to respond?

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Yes, if the Prosecution want to propose some redactions of that document, I'll listen to them. I'm only interested in the date at the top and the last paragraph.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we can ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we will adopt the same procedure. I don't think it is in the e-court, but I will make sure whether it is in e-court or not. I don't think it is. So what I suggest is that our intention is to admit it as -- however, having heard Mr. Haynes's statement, last statement, I suggest again once more that you meet, decide on or agree on the redactions and then it will be admitted as redacted upon agreement. All right? Thank you, Mr. Haynes, and thank you Mr. Vanderpuye. All right. Is Mr. Brunborg here?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, he is, Mr. President, and you are correct the agreement has been that this would be direct only and I would just -- I would -- tell the Court we are hoping to get him done relatively soon. This is the subject matter of demographics that could be a semester class and I will be taking him through it fairly broadly. And I know I don't need to do this, but I would invite you, of course, to ask any clarifying questions if you have them, and I know you will, but that's -- that's my intention, for direct only, and then he will come back after the Defence has had a -- had a chance to work with their own expert and cross-examine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wish to welcome you on behalf of the Tribunal.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you start giving evidence, you need to make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. The text is right in front of you. If you could kindly read that aloud and that will be your solemn undertaking with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. For the time being, you are only here for the examination-in-chief, and I therefore leave you in the capable hands of Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us your name and title, if any?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: My name is Helge Brunborg. Do you want me to spell it?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Sure.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: H-e-l-g-e, last name B-r-u-n-b-o-r-g.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And what is your profession?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I am a researcher in the field of demography.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where do you work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I work for Statistics Norway in Oslo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you tell us briefly what the field of demography is that you work in?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It's concerned about the study of population, population development and development -- and population structure including components like births and deaths.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I notice that you have got a lot of material in front of you that you have brought in. Were you asked to bring in some of that material by the Office of the Prosecutor?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we'll go over what that is and just let us know if you need to make any reference to it to help refresh your recollection. In fact, you have been employed by the Office of the Prosecutor as a demographer in the past, haven't you?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, from mid-1997 until the end of 1998, and as a consultant on a part-time basis for a couple of years after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Before we get to your work for the Office of the Prosecutor, can you tell us a bit about yourself? What recent projects have you been involved in that may have relevance to what you were doing or similar to what you were doing for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, most of my work is in Statistics Norway, and I am responsible for population projections for Norway. I am also a leader of a large project calls generations and gender programme, a large survey, but occasionally I have projects for other institutions and in other countries. Not so long ago, a couple of years ago I had a project in Afghanistan for UNFPA, the United Nations Fund for Population Activities to look at the possibilities of holding a census and the possibility of adding administrative data to that and I have also had worked on projects in countries like Palestine, Mozambique, Bangladesh, and Albania.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: As briefly as you can, give us the -- the guts of the kind of -- what this work involves. From the outside it's a little hard perhaps to understand what it is you are doing.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Demography it mostly about numbers and collecting numbers. And looking at the quality of numbers is a very important part of demography. It is an empirical science, in a way, but we also look at causal relationships between -- between these numbers. Say what affects births and deaths? What are the factors? Does education have anything to do with the development of births and deaths or other factors. On a recent project I would also like to know -- mention that I am involved in the international cooperation in a new field which we may call the demography of conflicts and violence or demography of armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. This new field, can you just briefly tell us how this new field, what it grew out of?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it grew out of my work here and together with colleagues initiated in working group of the International Unit for the Scientific Study of Population, we have organised seminars, published journals, and now a book came out last week, in fact, with papers from -- from the seminars. We study the consequences of armed conflict, which are mostly concerned with deaths but also migration and it also addresses the possible demographic causes of conflict which could be age bulges. Say, if there are many unemployed young youths then that could have -- could increase the probability of armed conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And have you testified as an expert at the ICTY before?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us in what cases?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I testified against Krstic on Srebrenica in the year 2000, against Blagojevic also in Srebrenica in 2003, against Milosevic in 2004 but that was not completed, and against Milutinovic et al in November of 2006 on Kosovo.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Have you published anything outside your work for the OTP about Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, I've written a couple of papers together with colleagues on Srebrenica called -- an article called, "Accounting for genocide" which has been published in an international journal called the European Journal for Population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let's get to your work for the -- for the OTP. When did you first come on to work for the OTP and what was your first assignment?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I started working here in June 1997 because the Office of the Prosecutor found out that they needed somebody who was knowledgeable about numbers, because there were many numbers concerning the -- the events in Yugoslavia, especially how many were killed. And they wanted somebody to look at these numbers and come up with the most reliable data. And my approach from the very beginning was to try to collect lists on -- with data on individuals, individual data because it is much harder to rely on the data of individuals, name, date of birth, place of birth, and so on, and what happened, date of death or date of disappearance. Then if you only have numbers in aggregate, say, 24 people were killed in such-and-such a place. That was the approach, to collect list of numbers on events, that is deaths, migrations, and also data on the population before and after the conflict started; before 1992 and after 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. At some point during your -- that work for the OTP, were you assigned specifically to assist the Srebrenica case?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think it was in the course in 1998 I was asked to compile a list of missing persons related to the events in Srebrenica in July 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And when you say missing persons, was that the -- the people that went missing after -- on or -- approximately on or after the fall of Srebrenica, mostly men?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And were you working with me on that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, including the team leader, Jean-Rene Ruez.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And can you tell us what you did to go about trying to identify that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I was advised that there was a list of -- collected by ICRC, the International Red Cross, of missing persons in all of Yugoslavia or mostly in all of Bosnia and that we should try to extract those missing persons that were related to the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So can you tell us what you learned about the ICRC list, first of all, and then we'll get into how you extracted potential Srebrenica missing from that overall list.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first I learned that the ICRC collected data on people who went missing during the conflict. In fact, in -- in most of the former Yugoslavia. First to help people unite with people who were relatives, family who got lost in the conflict, and later to try to identify the fate of those who went missing and did not reappear and who probably were dead. And I learned how they did that by people coming in, family members coming to report the victims; name, date of birth, and when they were last seen or what they think happened, where they were last seen, and other particulars about these persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You said that mostly family members came in. Was there some kind of quality control or requirement on who could report missing people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, in principle was only family members, and more than 95 per cent were reported by family members. There were a few others because in some cases whole families had disappeared so there was no family member to report.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And did you learn what locations the ICRC was able to take such reports of -- from family members or other close people?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Primarily in Tuzla because that's where most of the displaced persons in Srebrenica ended up, but also in other places all over Bosnia, in Sarajevo and other places.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And in your work and education as a demographer, had you had some familiarity with the work of the ICRC?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not with ICRC before, but these kind of records on individuals, with a name, date of birth, and type of event, was very familiar to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And we've obviously all heard of the ICRC, and -- but can you tell us what you learned a bit about their reputation, their ability, their mandate and doing this sort of work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, I knew from before of course that ICRC has a high reputation for being neutral and they really protect the neutrality so that they have access to -- to people on both sides of a conflict, to both parties. They can visit prisoners on the other side of the border, for example. So it is a humanitarian organisation, trying to help people in -- in conflicts.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Now, as I think it is also went known, much of their documentation and their material is private. How -- were you able to have access to the public material?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, in -- as part of the effort to locate people who have gone missing, they publish books on missing. I have a book here called, "Missing Persons on the Territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina," published in 1998, which in fact was the basis for our -- our study. And now they published a similar data on the internet.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you just tell us briefly what kind of information is contained in that book?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it tells name and sex of disappeared persons, father's name, place of birth, where they lived and where they disappeared. Yeah, and there is also a serial number. Those are the basic data.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This is information they're getting from family members or other close relatives?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get into that, the different volumes and how that affected your work a little later, I think. But can you first tell us, you have stated that the ICRC work that you were first learned about had to do with all of Bosnia. And so your first job was to separate the potential Srebrenica missing folks. How did you do that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We were advised that we should only select people for the Srebrenica list, people who were -- whose disappearance was related to the fall of Srebrenica. And the definition was that they should be on 12th of July or later, 1995, or disappearing at places that were close to Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: You are sure it was the 12th of July?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: 11th and -- sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And there are a few more who are accepted before. If it was before 11th of July, it was obvious that was related to the fall of Srebrenica, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you get these instructions from, to sort of -- identifying the -- this time-frame?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: From your team, sir.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And was there -- aside from the time-frame that we provided you, did we provide you any information about the location of where people went missing from -- to -- that would also limit it to Srebrenica potentially, anyway?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: You gave us a list of you could say relevant locations. Sometimes a municipality or an Opstina, sometimes a small place, hamlet, sometimes a place so small it wasn't on a map. So we had to ask -- or on the ICRC list, there were place that were on no maps so we had to ask people who were knowledgeable about the area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And were -- this first ICRC list, was that made available to you in electronic format?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did that help make your work possible?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we could not have worked if it had all been on paper.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you able it take that criteria that you were given and separate potential missing from Srebrenica on the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, can you -- did your work stop there?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No. Not at all. Because there were several versions of this list, a previous version, verse number three, and we worked with version number four. We combined these two versions. We had to delete those who appeared in both lists of course and we checked for errors and duplicates and came up with list of ICRC Srebrenica-related missing persons. We also -- we learned about another list assembled by something called PHR, Physicians for Human Rights, an American organisation, which were collecting ante-mortem database to help in identifying missing persons. So we merged actually two versions of their lists with the two versions of the ICRC list to come up with one consolidated list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you briefly tell us the -- how the -- the purpose of the ICRC list was different from the purpose of the PHR list, if there was a difference?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Originally I think the ICRC list was assembled to help perhaps locate surviving missing people, mostly, but that may have changed. And the PHR list was called an ante-mortem database and as the name says, they collected data on -- from family members on the victims also on physical characteristics, special clothing, special dental features, and so on, to help in -- when people were exhumed from mass graves because it was then known when they start in 1996 it was all known what happened. ICRC started already in July 1995 and it was really not known the extent and the character of the events in Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And I'm going to sort of skip to the end very briefly, and we'll get back, but if we could go to Exhibit P02423. And get that up on the screen, I see you have a hard copy of that in front of you. And is this something that was part of your report? Report, we see it as a source on the bottom of it. Can you just -- we see what it says. Can you first of all explain this number, 7.661?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: This is the total number of missing persons related to the fall of Srebrenica on the combined ICRC and PHR lists. It is slightly higher than the first list we prepared in the year 2000, which included 7.475 persons, I believe. 81, sorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Let me go there briefly. How many reports have you done in this continuing project for the OTP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: About six, six or eight or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And this is a reflection of the most recent one?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what -- let's go up to the next number, 23 still missing in PHR. What is that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is the number of people that we have learned nothing about. Nothing about their -- whether they survived or are dead. No bodies have been found, there are no strong witness statements saying that they were killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Then what closed cases, dead, 2.054, what is that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is the number of cases where the person has been declared dead. There is a death certificate usually issued by a judge. And -- and the body has usually then been delivered, turned over to the relatives.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I believe in your -- at Krstic that number was something like 70 at the very most, wasn't it? Or lower than that? Perhaps you should tell us what it was?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It was much lower -- no that number wasn't -- there wasn't such a number because the ICRC had no data on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. How is it now that that number is -- is 2.000? Can you tell us how that was determined?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, as time has passed there have been lots of exhumations and many bodies have been identified, and that is the major reason. Now it's already more than 10 years since the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Has another organisation come in -- into being that has helped in that process of identifying the dead?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Excuse me. Yes, in the year 2000 the ICMP, International Commission on Missing Persons, started working in Bosnia. It was established in 1996, and it has a mandate to -- to identify missing persons. And they -- they started working with a -- well, completely new technique. Because it was all based on the analysis, but they start with DNA analysis by first doing DNA extraction of bone samples of skeletons found in mass graves and later comparing those DNA reports with DNA reports of blood samples from relatives of victims. So ICMP with the out and announced and also asked close family members of victims to donate blood, on the average three people. You usually need more than one person, from one person, to be certain about close relations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We'll get a little more into that and how it affected your work a bit later, but that -- did that assist in closing cases and identifying confirmed dead as far as you know?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Vastly. In the year 2000, 70 people had been identified. Now more than 2.500.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And are you -- does your work continue? Will there be more data from the ICMP?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Oh, certainly. The work is continuing in Tuzla, and elsewhere, and new data are coming all the time. This report, the new report is based on data as of September 2005. Almost one and a half years ago. We have requested new data not received yet, but we are hoping to get new data soon and updates, make an addendum and update the list. We expect hundreds of new identified missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you -- what's the delay in getting the data? Roughly, if you know.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I don't know. We have sent a request, and we are hoping to get an answer very soon. We were told we would get it before Christmas, but it has been delayed. It is complicated, these are sensitive issues and the databases are very complicated technically. There are many difficult issues here. Also difficult ethical issues.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What are the difficult -- what kind of information is so sensitive? Can you just ...

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Of course. ICMP cannot go out with -- and release information on -- on dead people without having notified the dead people -- or the family members themselves. And it should go also not through -- only through forensic procedures but also through a court system so that a judge will then determine whether the information is sufficient to declare a person as dead.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's just finish up this -- this exhibit. We've talked about the old -- the closed cases. Then we get to the "still missing" info about dead, 318. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That means that is ongoing work, and there is probably -- there is probably a dead body but the process has not been completed, the identification process is not -- has not yet ended. Relatives may not have been notified, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And then we have "still missing," what is that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: At the top?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Those are the people we don't know anything about, other than they have gone missing, have been reported by relatives and there are no -- we have no information about their -- their survivorship, which has also been checked, by the way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: This new information from the ICMP, would you expect that that might eat away at that number a little bit?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Certainly, yes. We will see later during this testimony that that number has already come down.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And then down at the bottom, "total excluded entries, (all still missing): 12." What's that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: To make sure there were no survivors among the missing people, we searched electronically in databases of people after the war who were -- lived after the war. Mostly voters' lists collected by the OSCE during various elections in Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: To see, since a missing person cannot vote, that was the rationale for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We will get into that in a little more detail. Let me take you back. You've got that ICRC list, you've merged it with this PHR list, and have you done anything -- what is the first thing you do after you've done that to try to work on this data and see if it's any good?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the first anyone is to check there are any duplicates, to see if the same person was entered wrongly by different people, and so were counted as two or three missing persons instead of just one. So we had to compare then name, date of birth and so on. And this is not so easy because sometimes names are spelled differently, sometimes date of birth is given as slightly different, sometimes the date of birth is not known, the full date of birth is not known by family members, especially in a chaotic situation. Maybe the parents of a son only knew -- well, of course they -- they only remembered perhaps the year of birth. Or maybe it was a grandchild and they only remember the month and year of birth.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Was another problem particular to -- well, the former Yugoslavia and the number of names that were similar?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. That two people have the same name does not mean that they represent different persons. For example, there are more than 500 women with the name Fatima Hodzic in Bosnia. So we need to know more than just the name.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So with -- with these various problems you've outlined in this list, based on family members or grieving family members, were you able to do credible work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, because fortunately we -- we are able to get a copy of the 1991 census that is on the eve of the conflict there was a census in all of former Yugoslavia, including Bosnia, on the 31st of March, 1991, where everybody who lived in Bosnia was enumerated with data on name, first name, surname, father's name, date of birth, place of residence, marital status, household, et cetera. In addition to data on income and education and ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What did you learn about the accuracy or the reliability of that particular census? 1991 was a tough -- was a tough year.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, the -- the reliability is quite good. But there is one problem that was presented a challenge for us, and that is that the names were all full of mistakes. Because these forms were scanned, and if the handwriting was not so clear then there were often errors crept into the scanning. And because of the conflict there was no time to do the corrections. Now I should add, though, that names are not really important for a statistical exercise like a census. You don't need names to make statistics. But they collected the names to make sure that the enumeration of household and population was complete, because otherwise you do not know. You need names to check the completeness of the enumeration.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: In your experience had you dealt with these kind of census data or census data like this before?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not -- not with faulty names, no. But with my own country, Norway and in other countries I have dealt with census data, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Norway doesn't have faulty names in their census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We have personal identification numbers which are unique and of a good quality, high quality, right now.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. I was going to say after you and your staff had a chance to look at these, can you tell us what your -- what your view of that census was, but before I get to that, can you tell us what kind of staff you have. Is a question I should have asked earlier.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, first I worked alone for half a year, then I realised that there was a massive amount of work to -- because we could not do it all electronically, we had to do a lot of visual inspection of the data say of matches, if you did not know which Fatima Hodzic we were talking about. We needed to check visually. And if you have thousands or millions of people, then we need assistance. So I had several assistants in a row, mostly Norwegian graduate students that I knew before.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And where did you work and where did they work?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We worked at the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So let me get back to my original question --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Before going further, Mr. McCloskey, if you could kindly ask the witness to clarify -- to tell me the difference between the first item, "still missing," and the second last item, "still missing, PHR," which was not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Could you explain that to us?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I'm sorry for the confusion. All the data on this table comes from the ICRC list except that single line, PHR. PHR had something like between six and 7.000 missing people, but in the most recent ICRC version, almost all of the PHR data are included in ICRC lists. So the 23 missing people are reported to PHR only and not to ICRC.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. So can you tell us what -- after you had a chance to look at this, this census, what you thought of it for the purposes that you were asked to do?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Pretty good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And did you get that in electronic format as well?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we got it electronic format, 4.3 million records.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's a lot of people in the former Yugoslavia. You were tasked to basically deal with people missing from the Eastern Bosnia area; is that right? Were you able to use this census so you could stay within the Eastern Bosnia zone?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, we selected six or seven municipalities in Eastern Bosnia. At that time in 1998, 1999, then the computer capacity was a limitation. Today I think we wouldn't have need it. Now we don't need to do analysis just for a part of the population; we can all look at all of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Okay. So we've got this -- this list, the rough list from ICRC and a few from PHR. How does the census information help you in -- concerning the validity of the -- the ICRC list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We may use as an example perhaps an attempt to find living people among the missing people. And to do that we matched the missing lists with the voters' lists they collected after the war.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Well, you have jumped to voters' lists. Before we get to voters' lists, can you give me a little more direct -- what's the census do to help you? You may have explained it partly before, but you've got -- you've got this list of all these people that live all over Bosnia. How does that help you with this list of missing from family members?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, when we have the census, we know that if all the people on the missing list are in the census, we know that they are not made up or fictitious persons. They were at some time there was a -- at some point in time there were accusations that people reported people as missing to inflate the numbers. Now if you compare we can check then missing people with 1991 census to see if they were enumerated and then if they were there, then we know this existed. We can also get additional information that was not collected by the ICRC, which was collected by the census, in particular ethnicity and religion as reported by the enumerated people. And also the unique number, the so-called maticni broj, the unique identification number was used in the census, but not by ICRC. So we got additional information. Often we had a more complete date of birth than the ICRC collected.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What -- we've all learned how person that the father's name is in the former Yugoslavia. Did the ICRC list try to get the father's name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, father's name is there in most cases and also in the census.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Anything else in particular - I know we're jumping through this quickly - that the census helped you do in your analysis, and there may be other things.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, as I said, when we have certainly people with the same name and perhaps also the same father's name, the census can help us tell whether some names represent the same person or different persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. What else, what other databases or tools did you use to help check the validity of the ICRC list that you now have with the help of the census?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If I -- may I mention the voters' list now?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's where we are.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: And also there was a list collected much later on the displaced persons in Bosnia. But the voters' lists were collected by the OAC people, had to register to vote, and in 1997 and 1998, about 2.3 million people voted -- registered to vote, with name, but not name of father, I think. But the unique identification number in most cases, but not ethnicity. So it was partly overlapping information with the census, partly with the ICRC, but -- but a -- an important drawback of the -- of these voters' lists is that they only covered population over age 18, naturally, who are able to vote, have the right to vote. And also those who want to vote. So there were many not registered to vote because they were not interested or had left the country. There was also actually the campaign to register people who lived in other countries. But there were many people who did not register, but 2.3 million out of -- I don't remember how many. I think 70 per cent on average of the population registered to vote.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And did you look at the names of people registered to vote to see if they were on the missing list? Because people are registering to vote, they -- probably not missing.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. That was the hypothesis that if there were many -- many survivors who were wrongly reported as missing, then they might register to vote. So we did -- we did comparisons with voters registered.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think it's time for a break and we can get into that voters' registration details.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are correct. We will have a 25-minute break starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Mr. Brunborg, and Mr. McCloskey. Go ahead, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. We left off, you had just begun to talk about the -- a couple of voters' registration lists, and how you wanted to check to see if there were anybody that registered to vote that was on the missing list. But I believe you said that the voters' registration list didn't have fathers' names; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, I think that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So what -- how were you able to use a Yugoslav, former Yugoslav document that didn't have fathers' names?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We did have the date of birth and also the maticni broj, the unique identification number, and municipality of residence, although that changed for many, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. So did you find that you were able to make a useful comparison between the voters' list and -- and your developing missing list?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, but it was very hard to do the matching because for some people, as was indicated, there was not a whole lot of information. So at the first go at it you could get several thousand matches, but then you were limiting it and then we ended up with a few cases where -- which we scrutinised very closely to see if this was a true match or a false match. And if I may mention an example of our methodology?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: We do have some exhibits of true matches and false matches. Is that -- a good time to go to that, I think. The Exhibit is 65 ter 572, and it's I believe a document that you have developed in your report, and can you just go down this for us. Based on real data, but modified for protection of identity. Why do you modify it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, we did not want this to -- the names of -- of these real person to be known. They may want to protect their privacy.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Can you explain this for us?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. After the electronic matching we found many possible matches, saying that the two records representing the same person. We that that according to the ICRC list there is a person, Mensur Gabelic, father's name Avdo, born in 1970, and in the voters' list, 1997, there is also a Mensur, but spelled not Gabelic, but with a Q instead. That is obviously a misprint, so that was corrected. But need to know about that to correct that electronically. However, without the father's name in the voters' register because it was not entered and the year -- date of birth is slightly different from the year of birth recorded in the ICRC lists. So what he we did, we went to the census and looked for all the Gabelic family, Mensur Gabelic, and you found one, father's name was Avoo with two Os, not "-do". There was nobody else with the names and date of birth similar to that, so we conclude that this is a true match. Those two records above represent the same person, and although there are some differences in the records, minor differences, so would he conclude that this person is a possible or potential survivor although he was registered missing, and he was then deleted from our list of missing persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: To be on the safe side. Now, the other thing that could have happened of course was that this person was wrongly registered to vote. Somebody might have known that this person was registered missing, in fact it was public information and misused this person's identity to vote, to get an extra vote, that's possible. But we don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But to be on the safe side, you pulled that --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: -- person. Do you know how many matches you had like that?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Nine out of seven and a half thousand.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Statistically, what does that mean?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: It is of no significance. If there had been hundreds, yes, we would have been concerned. But if you don't do this correctly, you could get several thousand matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I think the next exhibit is an example of a -- what you have called an example of a false match. That's Exhibit 573, if we could get that one up there. Walk us through this one.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: According to the ICRC, there is an Abdula Delic, his father's name was Husein, born in 1955, and this was then seemingly matched with a voters' register person called Abdula Delic, father's name not listed, as before, year of birth 1955. So this seems to be the same person. But then we checked and we found that there were two persons by that name in the census, one where the father's name was Husein, the other father's name was Kemal, both born in 1955; moreover, the son of Kemal's number is identical to the voters register number. So these represent different records, the son of Husein did not register to vote, he's still missing, and he was not excluded from the list. So this shows how useful it is to have the access to a database with a complete population.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, having those few examples of your methodology, is there anything else you would like to say about methodology before we talk a bit about the results?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: We can come back to that, I think. You need to do lots of corrections, like correcting names, for example, misspellings in names according to Bosnian naming traditions, and we spent a lot of time on that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Then let's go to the next exhibit, which is P02424, it's another graph, and I think if -- once that gets up there -- apparently it's in colour so it takes a bit longer. But ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Since we have a pause, Your Honour, if I could just direct your attention to line 75 -- or page 75, line 21, I thought the witness said, although it wasn't not recorded there, but it may be significant, at least for our questioning, when he said, "It is of no significance. If there were hundreds we would have been concerned," and then I thought after that he said if you do not do the -- if you do not do this correctly you can get several thousand matches. I just want to confirm that that's what he said. I thought he did, I wrote it down, and I looked up, and it wasn't there. It may be significant for us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Brunborg, you have heard Mr. Ostojic's submission. Do you agree?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That is correct, but I hope I am not misunderstood, the statement is not misunderstood.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In what sense?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: That if it is done correctly, you got nine matches. That is the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And I think we've given enough examples to show the kind of crunching and numbers and reviewing that you have done in order to do it correctly. Is there anything else --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment before you move ahead. I am not familiar with the set-up, so I wouldn't be able to know, but in Bosnia and Serbia or wherever in the territory of the ex-Yugoslavia, Mr. Brunborg, did they have or do they have an office which is the archive of identity cards?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: I don't -- I'm not familiar with the archive of identity cards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: An office where all records relating to identity cards are kept, in other words.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: It is possible that the so-called MUP, the Ministry of the Interior, also kept records of identity cards, but I am not familiar. But they -- as I said they introduced the ID number in 1981 and it was used in 1981 census, 1991 census, but not as widely as in the Nordic countries, for example.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My question is, if one were to go and search for a person under his identity card number would you find any records that would then give you all the details that you would normally have elsewhere in Europe, for example, or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Not to my knowledge.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. That -- that is a topic that the investigation may be able to help -- help you with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One further question. By any chance do the ID numbers correspond to the birth certificate records or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The date of birth is part of the ID number, and the place of birth is also part, or the region of birth or the region where the person lived in 1981. And the gender is also part of the number.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just on a related -- related topic that I recalled, were you directed by the -- well, by the -- the investigation initially not to use any missing lists from either of the parties, the Muslims, the Croats or the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not directly. I did collect some lists of that kind, but they have not -- data from those lists have not been included in our work to -- to make sure that there was absolutely no question of the -- about non-neutrality. And, anyway, most of the data are -- those data are included in the ICRC lists anyway. But it could have added if some deaths are missing persons. So -- so which means that the numbers representing here are absolutely minimum numbers. The real numbers are likely to be somewhat higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, you bring that up. Do you have something called a margin of error in this analysis?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not really. But we think that it's close to minimum, so the chance that it is lower than this is very small. The chance that it is higher is quite large, that the real number is higher.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: So it is at the end of the tail, you could say.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Well, then let's -- the colour shot is up. So this -- tell us what this -- what this is.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: This shows us the age distribution of the Srebrenica-related missing and dead persons.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Were you asked to do this by the investigation?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Not originally. This is a sort of a very natural for a demographer to do and you will see that we have done it in five-year age groups, but the OTP did, in fact, ask us to break it down by the age groups given below, children and adults and old people. And we noticed that the majority is in sort of regular adults, you could say, 16 to 60, and -- but also a sizeable number of children and old people, and we also noticed that the number of women is very small; 68 out of 7.661, which is less than one per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Let's go to the next -- the next exhibit, which is 2426. And before we get there, I believe it incorporates some data from the ICMP information that you had compiled more recently. You have talked about that a bit. But can you -- when this -- when this picture comes up, can you explain what this graph depicts and a little bit more about this ICMP data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, as I said, ICMP's task is to identify people from mass graves. And this is ongoing work, the first person was identified in 2001. As of September 2005, that identified 2.591 people related to the fall of Srebrenica. And it's the age distribution of those that we see in the black bars here. And the red bars represent the age distribution of the ICRC list, which we saw previously, except that here we have a percentage distribution; the previous picture showed absolute numbers. We noticed that the age distributions are very similar. Which indicates that they come from the same population, that the identified people come from the population of missing people who are still in the -- most still in the graves. We also see that the identified are -- proportions are lower for the young people between 15 and 24 and some -- yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just to be clear you are making reference to where there is a lot more red than black from 15 to 19 and 19 to 24?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: What does that mean, you think?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That means that young people have been less identified to a less extent, so far, than older people. And the -- I think the explanation of that is that young people -- more of the young people went trekking through the woods than the old people, who mostly went to Potocari with their families. They did not trek through the woods because they wanted to be with the families and because they were not in the health condition to do that. So -- so that more of the old people have been exhumed and identified than the young people.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Though the exhumation process and the identifying of remains is -- is -- is still going on as we speak, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes, as of 11 July last year they had found about 600 more, identified 600 more than the year before. And now we have almost one and a half years after September 2005, so we expect almost 1.000 more identified. So we should then be in the area, region of three and a half thousand persons identified, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brunborg, I think from what you have testified on this chart here, where the red line or column is higher than the black one, is abundantly clear. What perhaps needs some explanation is where the black line shows a higher percentage than the red line. In other words, more -- a higher percentage of exhumed and identified persons than those established in parentheses as missing and dead. If you could explain that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes, it's exactly because it is so much the percentage exhumed and identified among young people is so much lower that then naturally the percentage identified among older people become higher. You remember that the percentages add up to -- to 100 here. So that is the reason.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not still not understanding correctly. If we take the sector dealing with young people aged between 15 and 19, I agree with you that the chart shows that the number of -- or the percentage of exhumed and identified persons is lower than the percentage of those found missing and dead. But if we go, for example, to the age bracket 55 to 59 or to 60 to 64 and 65 to 69, and also the age bracket 45 to 49, and 50 to 54, you will see that the percentage of exhumed -- exhumed and identified persons is larger than the percentage of missing and dead. This is what I would like you to explain.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: This is because more of the elderly were presumed -- went missing and buried in places where there's been a higher degree of exhumations and also of identification. I think this becomes clear if you look at the next picture, because as I said, many of the -- those who went missing in Potocari were much older than -- than the general population.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But my question is: According to this chart the red represents missing and dead, according to the ICRC.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's take the bracket 45 to 49.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Mm-hmm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. There is roughly just over eight per cent of the entire missing population that belonged to this age bracket, 45 to 49. My question is, how come that more bodies than eight per cent were exhumed? Because I would expect that exhumations would always fall at least and reach the maximum as maximum the number of missing and dead ICRC persons in that particular bracket. This is what is intriguing me.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Now I understand your concern. The sum of the red bars adds up to about 7.600. The sum of the black bars adds up to 2.500, because so far about one third of the missing have been exhumed and identified.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: That was the very question I was coming to, but do you have the -- have a table comparing the absolute numbers? What's the significance comparing the percentage in one graph, so the confusion may arise from that fact.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: We do not -- it's in the report, in this executive summary and the report, the absolute number is given. If this graph had been made with absolute numbers instead of percentages, all the black bars would have been much lower than the red bars. We did make that, but it looked some kind of strange because it would be, sort of, on the average one third of the red bars. So this was to show the similarity of the age distributions that we used percentage instead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Let's go to the next -- the next one, which is 2427. Will take a while to come up. And I -- it's entitled, "Proportion of missing men from --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, it's showing the correct one now and the title is different.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm sorry. I jumped ahead of myself. Got the right number, and this one is entitled, "Age distribution of identified persons reported on the 2005 OTP list as missing persons from Potocari." Okay. What is this?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: In a way this is exactly the same graph as the previous graph except that we have only looked at people who went missing in Potocari. It shows that the distributions are very different because the men who went missing from Potocari are on average much older than the general population. As I said, many of the young men that went trekking through the woods, whereas the older men went with their families and -- or sometimes grandchildren to Potocari. And more of them have been then exhumed and identified. So we have to be careful when drawing conclusions because the age pattern is very different in different locations.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Do you have the number of men missing from Potocari that you used to make this graph?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: If you allow me for a second, it is also given in the report, excuse me. Yeah, on page 22 of the report of 16 November 2005, table 6, from 2070 went missing from Potocari. The second highest place of disappearance is forests, where 1.085 went missing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: What was the sum of black columns in absolute numbers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: The sum of the black column, I'm sorry, I don't have -- let me see. Closed cases, it must be approximately 260. No, sorry, approximately 700, because those are the identified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And how did you determine that number? Why do you pick 700 for the black -- the blacks?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: These are the closed cases, ICRC data and not the ICMP data but they are very similar. So I would have to check and look up the ICMP data which I think may be given in the report of 21st November.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Well, I don't think we need to go into that now. The next -- the next graph is number 2425. Okay. Can you tell us what this means?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yeah, first I think this is very interesting graph. We have been able to produce it because we were able to link the missing people on the ICRC list with the census. There is one word missing from the title - they were Muslims - should be mentioned, included. This shows the proportion of Muslim men who lived in Srebrenica in 1991 who went missing in 1995. And it is really those who were resident, they are matched on a individual basis, one to one basis. So for each person who were enumerated -- for each Muslim man who were enumerated in Srebrenica in 1991, we could see whether that person was reported as missing in 1995. And we see that on average about one third of the Muslim men enumerated in 1991 went missing in 1995. Up to 50 per cent, in fact, for the middle ages, between 49 and 55 went missing. These are really underestimates of the proportions who went missing, because it does not take into account that many Muslim men left Srebrenica before 1995. Either because they went elsewhere, and there are also several people who died from natural and other causes. Same, especially among the elderly, where 10 -- as many died from natural causes who were -- who disappeared in 1995. So the real figures are proportions are probably much higher. But the proportions are staggering, because we see that one third of the Muslim men went missing and are probably dead, and up to 50 per cent.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. Apart from the people from Srebrenica, men from Srebrenica that had left Srebrenica prior to or in the early part of the war before -- do you exclude from this list men from Srebrenica who may have died in action between 1992 and 1995?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Certainly, yeah. They're not there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And on what basis? This is why I want to have this clear.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Because the enumerator, if you may, only reported people missing as related to the events around the 11 of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Moreover, another group is also excluded from this chart, and that is men from other municipalities who were in -- located in Srebrenica in July 1995, say from Bratunac or Zvornik because they are not listed here. They are listed as where they were enumerated in 1991, so we could make similar charts for other areas but the bars would be much lower, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Did your review of this list make an effort to determine if anybody on that ICRC list had actually died before July 11th, 1995?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Oh, certainly. We compared lists of military deaths, they were also -- there was critique from -- from other sources in Republic of Srpska and in Belgrade that claim that we were including people who had died before 1995 from -- killed in action or in combat or for other causes. And we checked all those and we didn't find any.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. And just --

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: They were excluded if we ...

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: If I can just briefly help outline some -- something that may make some of this area a little clearer. You wrote your first report for Krstic in February 2000; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And then you wrote the report that I believe we referred to as the rebuttal report in 2004. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That is correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And in your -- now we have the latest report is 16 November 2005. Now, can you tell us with -- having in mind that -- is the report, the latest one, 16 November, is that designed to encompass the entire report or is it volume 2?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, it's designed to include the entire report. The 2000 report and their findings and data that were collected afterwards. For example, this chart we see here, we did not make in 2000 because we hadn't done the match between the missing and the census population 1991 for all of Bosnia or for all of Srebrenica. We did not have the technology to do it.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But does -- is everything in this 16 November 2005 report included in the February 2000 report?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: No, because we have findings and there are a few issues that were included in the 2000 report that we did not repeat in the 2005 report. For example, on -- if I may mention, on page 10, I believe, in the 2000 report we refer to what's -- it's called attempts at undermining the ICRC list of missing persons and we refer to books and articles and reports criticising our findings, or criticising, actually, the ICRC lists.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can you give us just one example of -- of one such criticism that perhaps we haven't talked about?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, it was claimed that there were many people who registered to vote, hundreds of people who registered to vote who were also on the missing lists.
