According to the 1996 list of voters. But that is no surprise, because the 1996 list of voters was exactly the 1991 census. It was the same. There was no new collection of -- there was no new registration of voters, they just used the 1991 census, so then there is no surprise you find many people on both lists. That's one example. So you have to be knowledgeable about what happened how the registration of voters was done.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So just for the Court that for some specific criticisms that came from some organisations, I think, the Belgrade law centre is one organisation, there is a more detailed analysis of those criticisms in the 2000 report; in fact, there is none of that is in the more recent report; is that right?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Now, you mentioned the rebuttal 2004 report. Rebuttal of what? What's that about?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, in the Blagojevic trial then the -- the Defence had hired an expert demographer from Belgrade who got access to the data, our list, the ICRC list, and claimed to find several duplicates and other errors also in the ICRC list or OTP list.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And that expert was provided access to the same material you had had access to, the census and other things?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: She was given a computer and with access to the census and the OTP list in this very building.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: And can you tell us, did she make some valid points?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Her three points were that first that there were many duplicates and she actually -- she claimed there were five certain duplicates and another five likely duplicates in the missing list, meaning that there were some persons who were included twice. Twice. And unfortunately she was right. There were, in fact, some duplicates, we had already found them, we had detected them, we marked them, but through an oversight we forgot to remove them. They were there for organisational reasons and also we had to decide if there are two records and they are almost identical, say the date of birth is slightly different, we had to decide on which record to remove. And that had been forgotten in all of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. Have those been removed now in your latest data?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes and we did an additional, very thorough analysis of duplicates and it came up with a total of 24. And they were removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So an additional 24 from the 10 the expert -- other expert had found?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Well, only eight of her duplicates were valid, actually.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Two were false matches.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Okay. You have mentioned that she had three points. That being point one. What were the other two points?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: The other two points was that there were fictitious persons in the missing list. She mentioned some names. Name and date of birth. We checked the census and found the particulars of those persons. So they were enumerated in 1991 and it is quite unlikely that they were fictitiously enumerated. So we refuted that claim, I think. The third one that there were survivors and we checked that but we did not find any survivors except for those we had included already, those nine that were possible survivors in the voters' list, 1997/1998. But we have come to believe that it is more likely that they were not survivors, but they were wrongly registered to vote. In fact, later it has been found that two of those nine are -- were dead. So somebody had misused their identities or there has been a mix-up, an error.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Did you find any -- any significant misuse of -- of these data, people putting fake names into the ICRC list or false names into the voters' lists? I mean you have mentioned there are been a couple of anomalies if you want to call it that, but did you find anything significant that would affect your conclusions?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: On the missing list we haven't found any example of that. On the voters' list, possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. And it's my understanding that same expert will be -- is reviewing your material now, and I'm sure you look forward to seeing her latest critique.

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Very much. This is the kind of quality control that we welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: All right. Just to give her the credit of her name, do you remember her name?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Mrs. Radovanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Okay. If I could -- to make the record clear, the 12 February 2000 report is 65 ter 571. The 25 August 2004 rebuttal report is P02412. The -- there is a November 16th, 2005 updated report which is P02413. And that updated report has an addendum which is dated 21 November 2005, and I believe that addendum is -- is a confidential addendum. Can you tell us just briefly what is the addendum to your latest report and why is it confidential?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Because it includes data on individuals from ICMP and to protect the privacy on those individuals it's presented under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I didn't read that number, which is P02416. Now, this has been a pretty quick lesson or a testimony, I should say, on this topic. Is there anything -- this is your last chance on direct to offer anything in your -- in your process or your -- that you think I -- we've left out. Obviously we've left out a lot, but is there anything you would like to say in conclusion?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: I think we should repeat that this is an ongoing process, that new data are coming all the time, the new exhumations, the identification process is going on. So there is no final number. For posterity it would be nice to be -- very good to have a final number, but it will be quite a while before we get the final numbers. It will slowly increase, sometimes it will drop a little bit when you find a few errors, but then it will increase slowly. And the number of identified persons will increase dramatically, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Is that unfortunately linked to the continuing exhumations of the bodies still in the ground?

utterances.speaker: HELGE BRUNBORG
utterances.text: Yes. Certainly.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm finished for this evening, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. McCloskey. Would it cause your office any problem if you could provide us with a hard copy of the relevant reports? One each, in other words.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Not at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: In case of expert report or any documents of extensive volume in the future.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: The actual missing list, we had one for the last trial of the seven -- roughly 7.400 which we have hard copies of with -- the 7.600 we don't have the hard copy as yet, but it's electronic, but we -- I've asked to get one of those and we'll provide that as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Brunborg.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry, if I may.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, certainly.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Sorry. If I may repeat that I would like to make an addendum based on new reports from -- from ICMP and we intend to do that within a month or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I thank you so much. On behalf of the Tribunal I should like to thank you for having been kind enough to come and give testimony in this case. And on behalf of everyone, I wish you a safe journey back to Norway. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, Witness 45.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, we have another witness, if you would like another witness. Okay. Mr. Thayer will be up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Exhibit D73, it seems that the Prosecutor has nothing else, the three pages of the Oric case will be put in the file instead of this exhibit. As far as I'm concerned, if it is acceptable for the Chamber, instead of D73, I prefer the three pages of the Oric case, 3.078 until 3.378 until 3.381 [as interpreted] in the file. If it is acceptable by the members of the Chamber.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose what shows in the transcript as D73 is 5D173. That's what you're referring to, aren't you? What are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. 5D173, indeed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't remember the Oric case by heart, but which three pages of the Oric case are you referring to? Because we didn't hear anything about any -- any transcripts from that case, from that trial. Seems somewhat unclear in my mind, this is why I'm asking.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Pages of the Oric case, the transcript, to which there was a reference made during the objection to the content of these pages, indeed the same as the exhibit I referred to. I found it on IDS, apparently Prosecutor had these three pages of the Oric case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. We'll leave that pending until Monday. What are we going to do with the documents? I suppose -- the Brunborg documents.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, the -- the agreement was we would -- he'd come back at -- for cross-examination after their expert has had a chance to review everything. I guess we put them on ice until that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wanted to make that clear because I didn't want to make the impression that we were leaving an unfinished symphony. Next witness is 45?

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good evening, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Good evening.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And welcome to this Tribunal. You are just about to start your evidence. Our rules require that before you do so you make a solemn declaration that you will be testifying the truth. Madam Usher is handing you the text of the solemn declaration. Please read it out and that will be your declaration with us.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, sir. Please take a seat and make yourself comfortable. You will only be about 10 to 12 minutes today and then you will return on Monday. I just wanted to put your mind at rest that we have granted you two protective measures that the Prosecution sought for you, namely the use of a pseudonym and also facial distortion. I trust these have been explained to you and that they are to your satisfaction.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Thayer will go first, and then we will continue on Monday. Mr. Thayer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Good evening, sir. Madam Usher will be handing you a piece of paper. I will ask you to read it to yourself and confirm that your name is printed next to the number PW-155. For the record, the sheet is P02401. And if could you just confirm orally that your name is there, if it is there, sir.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-155
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. THAYER
utterances.text: Mr. President, while the pseudonym sheet is being handed around, if we could move into private session?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's move into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. We have run out of time, so we have to stop here. You will return Monday morning when we will proceed with -- hopefully conclude with your testimony. Thank you. Have a nice evening, everyone.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: to be reconvened on Monday, the 5th day of February, 2007, at 9.00 a.m. 25
